content:
Hello, I am looking for an efficient way to prove an equation, roughly,
compile ast = bytecode
where ast in AST in Lean is 2MB, and bytecode is a literal artifact just under a megabyte.
I have a correctness theorem for the compiler, and this equation allows me to lift properties.

I am trying to avoid extra axioms. So I avoided native_decide and got a proof with 55k Lean files and 2 hrs build time (on 32 cores), but I am not sure if that's the right way.

How have others got these large concrete computation kernel-checked?

(I'm seeing 15% chance this is off-topic. I didn't see anywhere else that fits better. I guessed program verification often involves large ASTs and people here might have relevant experiences.)
You could attempt using cbv, potentially with cbv_eval theorems if required
If you want to be more experimental and don't shy away from meta programming you could also try to adapt https://github.com/nomeata/lean-cwp/ (maybe your favorite agent can help)

If you want to stick to rfl there are a bunch of tricks about how to make code reduce more efficiently in the kernel. The https://competition.sair.foundation/competitions/lean-kernel-challenge/evaluation-setup competition is all about that, maybe we'll learn more tricks this way

Thank you! cwp seems to have an interesting elab vs kernel costs. For my context (running a competition about compilation challenge), elaboration can be file-parallel but comparator is single process.

My roadmap contains making a machine-code port of con-leche with proofs.
Sounds fun! What's your machine level semantics?

For now the semantics that CakeML uses because I've been porting CakeML codebase, empirically keeping the same output, and visually keeping statements similar.

For the immediate project, I've only had RISC-V backend ported. Comparison with Sail RISC-V extraction looks like one needs to be careful about certain points. For ARMv8 it looks promising: https://drops.dagstuhl.de/entities/document/10.4230/LIPIcs.ITP.2022.20

I see a lot of strategic thinking is involved. For instance, when it's about inserting an element to a list, a derivation of the big-step semantics becomes as tall as the list, and chasing that might not be easier than reducing the term.

If the compiler itself can be organized like compilation by evaluation, could be a very nice fit for cwp.

To be honest I'm missing trusted computers in other settings. ACL2 reduces terms without producing proof terms (seeing only types of open goals). Rocq has a trusted vm. HOL4 got cv_compute.

https://peregrine-project.github.io/ would allow you to compiler the boolean program "compile ast = bytecode" to many backends (some more verified than others). It would give you both differential testing and a more verified backend than lean currently has.
Do you have the Lean boolean somewhere in isolated sources?

Nothing isolated.

I'll try (1) to use current Lean kernel in a performant way, or (2) get enough insights to argue for extending the kernel.

Naive use of cwp didn't help, might be a skill issue but above mentioned list-insertion style computation is involved.

I have a suspicion that the current Lean kernel's treatment of Nat already allows cv_compute style acceleration. Namely to compile certain calculation into calculation on only Nat and pairs, and reflect.
The reason for avoiding cross-language translation comes from preference for encapsulated complexity.
